title: Scope, Closures and Functions: The JavaScript Behind React
objectives: Explain lexical scope and the difference between var, let and const.
Define a closure and describe what a function 'remembers' after its outer function returns.
Use closures to create private state, the same idea React hooks rely on.
Recognise the stale-closure bug and explain why it appears in React event handlers and effects.
Answer common closure interview questions, including the classic loop-with-setTimeout puzzle.
definition: Scope decides where a variable can be read. JavaScript uses lexical scope: a function can see the variables that existed where it was written, not where it is called. A closure is a function together with the variables from its surrounding scope that it keeps alive, so it can still read and update them after the outer function has finished running.

theory.heading: Lexical scope and block scope
theory.body: Every function creates a new scope, and with let and const every block ({ ... }) does too. When JavaScript looks up a name it searches the current scope, then the enclosing one, and so on up to the global scope; this chain is fixed by where the code is written. var is function-scoped and hoisted with the value undefined, which caused many bugs; let and const are block-scoped and sit in a 'temporal dead zone' until their declaration runs. Modern React code uses const by default and let only when a variable must be reassigned.
points: var: function scope, hoisted as undefined, can be redeclared.
let: block scope, can be reassigned, cannot be read before its declaration.
const: block scope, cannot be reassigned (the object it points to can still be mutated).
Lookup goes outward through enclosing scopes, never inward.

theory.heading: What a closure is
theory.body: When an inner function refers to a variable of an outer function, the engine keeps that variable alive as long as the inner function exists. The inner function 'closes over' the variable. This is not a copy of the value: it is a live reference to the binding, so updates made by one closure are visible to every other closure that shares the same scope.
points: Closures are created every time a function is created, not only when it is returned.
Each call to the outer function creates a fresh set of variables, so two counters do not share state.
Closures enable data privacy: the variable cannot be reached except through the returned functions.

theory.heading: Why closures matter in React
theory.body: A function component is just a function that runs on every render. Event handlers, effect callbacks and callbacks passed to children are closures created during that render, so they see the props and state of that specific render. This is why React feels predictable, and also why a handler created in an old render can read an old value: the 'stale closure' problem. useState itself is built on the same idea: React stores state outside your function and hands each render a snapshot.
points: Each render has its own props, state and handlers (a snapshot).
A stale closure reads values from an earlier render, often inside setInterval or an effect with missing dependencies.
Fixes: functional updates (setCount(c => c + 1)), correct dependency arrays, or a ref for the latest value.

theory.heading: Arrow functions and this
theory.body: Arrow functions do not have their own this, arguments or prototype; they use this from the enclosing scope. In class components developers bound methods or used arrow class fields to keep this pointing at the component. Function components avoid this entirely, which is one reason closures replaced this-based patterns in modern React.
points: Arrow functions are concise and ideal for callbacks such as items.map(item => ...).
Regular functions get this from how they are called; arrows take it from where they are defined.

theory.heading: Costs and pitfalls
theory.body: Closures keep their captured variables in memory, so a long-lived closure (for example a listener that is never removed) can keep large objects alive and cause leaks. In React, creating new closures on every render is normally cheap; it only matters when a new function identity breaks memoisation of a child, which is what useCallback addresses later in the course.
points: Remove event listeners and clear timers in cleanup functions.
New function identity each render is fine unless a memoised child or a dependency array depends on it.

example.title: A counter with private state
example.body: makeCounter returns three functions that share one private variable. Nothing outside can change count except through these functions, and two counters made by separate calls are independent because each call creates a new scope.

use_cases.title: React hooks
use_cases.description: useState, useEffect and custom hooks rely on functions that capture the props and state of the render in which they were created.

use_cases.title: Event handlers
use_cases.description: onClick={() => removeItem(item.id)} closes over item, so each button knows which item it belongs to.

use_cases.title: Debounce and throttle
use_cases.description: Utility functions keep the timer id in a closure so repeated calls can cancel the previous timer.

use_cases.title: Module privacy
use_cases.description: Factory functions and modules hide internal variables and expose only a small public API.

use_cases.title: Memoisation
use_cases.description: A memoize helper stores its cache in a closure so that results persist between calls without a global variable.

demonstration.description: The classic interview puzzle: the same loop prints different results with var and let. With var there is one shared binding that has reached 3 when the timers fire; with let each iteration gets a fresh binding that each callback closes over.
demonstration.output:
var 3
var 3
var 3
let 0
let 1
let 2

takeaways: JavaScript scope is lexical: decided by where code is written, not where it runs.
Prefer const, use let when reassigning, and avoid var in modern code.
A closure keeps a live reference to outer variables, not a copy of their values.
Every React render creates new closures that see that render's props and state.
Stale closures are fixed with functional state updates, correct dependencies or refs.
Long-lived closures can leak memory, so always clean up listeners and timers.

interview.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
interview.answer: A closure is a function bundled with references to the variables in the scope where it was defined. It can read and update those variables even after the outer function has returned.
interview.explanation: A strong answer adds a small example (a counter factory) and stresses that the closure holds a live reference, not a snapshot copy.

interview.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
interview.answer: var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined; let and const are block-scoped and in the temporal dead zone until declared. const prevents reassignment of the binding but does not make objects immutable.
interview.explanation: Interviewers often follow up with 'can you push to a const array?' (yes), so mention that const is about the binding, not the value.

interview.question: Why does a for loop with var and setTimeout print the same number three times?
interview.answer: var creates a single function-scoped variable shared by all iterations. The callbacks run after the loop ends, when the shared variable already holds its final value. let creates a new binding per iteration, so each callback sees its own value.
interview.explanation: Mention the event loop: timers run only after the synchronous loop completes. Offering the let fix and the older IIFE fix shows depth.

interview.question: What is a stale closure in React and how do you fix it?
interview.answer: It is a callback that captured state or props from an earlier render and therefore reads an outdated value, for example setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1)) inside an effect with an empty dependency array. Fix it with a functional update (setCount(c => c + 1)), by listing the value in the dependency array, or by reading the latest value from a ref.
interview.explanation: This connects a JavaScript fundamental to real React bugs, which is exactly what front-end interviewers want to see.

interview.question: Can closures cause memory leaks? Give an example.
interview.answer: Yes. If a closure that references a large object is stored somewhere long-lived, such as a window event listener or an interval that is never cleared, the object cannot be garbage-collected. Removing listeners and clearing timers in cleanup functions prevents it.
interview.explanation: Link the answer to useEffect cleanup, which you will study on Day 11.

practice.title: Counter factory with private state
practice.objective: Use closures to give each counter its own private value, start and step, exactly like independent component instances keep independent state.
practice.statement: Implement makeCounter(start, step) that returns inc, dec, reset and get functions sharing a private value. Then process commands. 'create <name> <start> <step>' creates a counter (print 'error: <name> exists' if the name is taken). 'inc <name>' adds step, 'dec <name>' subtracts step, 'reset <name>' returns to start, and 'get <name>' prints '<name>=<value>'. Any command on an unknown counter prints 'error: <name> not found'.
practice.input_format: First line: N, the number of commands. Next N lines: one command each.
practice.output_format: One line for every get command and every error, in order.

example.input:
6
create a 0 1
create b 10 5
inc a
inc a
dec b
get a

constraints: start and step are integers (step may be negative).
Names are single words without spaces.
explanation: makeCounter declares value with let; the four returned arrow functions close over it, so it stays private and alive.
Each create call runs makeCounter again, producing a fresh scope, so counters never share values.
reset works because start is also captured by the closure.
The command loop looks up the counter by name and calls the matching method, printing only for get and errors.

quiz.question: What does a JavaScript closure capture from its outer scope?
options: Live references to the outer variables
Nothing; closures only work in classes
A frozen copy of each variable's value
quiz.explanation: A closure keeps live bindings. If the outer variable changes, the closure sees the new value.

quiz.question: What does this code print?
quiz.explanation: var gives one shared binding. The timers run after the loop finishes, when i is 3.

quiz.question: Inside useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, []), the count goes to 1 and stops. Why?
options: The cleanup function runs every second
The interval callback closes over count from the first render, which is always 0
setInterval does not work inside React
setCount is asynchronous and drops updates
quiz.explanation: The empty dependency array means the effect, and its closure over count = 0, is created once. Use setCount(c => c + 1) instead.

quiz.question: Which statement about const is correct?
options: It throws a TypeError because list is const
It works: const prevents reassignment, not mutation
quiz.explanation: const fixes the binding. The array object can still be mutated, which is why React relies on immutability by convention, not on const.

quiz.question: Why are two counters created by separate calls to makeCounter() independent?
options: Because each call creates a new scope with its own variables
Because the counters are stored in different files
Because JavaScript copies functions when they are returned
quiz.explanation: Every invocation of the outer function creates fresh local variables, so each returned closure set has its own state.
